summary: Shares the latest ARPANET maps, both geographic and logical, together with a list of Hosts connected. The maps show IMPs and TIPs and the status of the computers on the net as of mid-December 1973.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a set of maps of the network, showing where the machines are and how they are connected, plus a list of the computers.

questions: what is a very distant host
subtitle: A December 1973 snapshot of the ARPANET maps and the list of connected Hosts.

tldr.problem: The network community needed a current picture of which computers were attached to the ARPANET and where.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists Hosts with octal and decimal addresses, official Hostnames, computers and status, and describes the geographic and logical maps (not reproduced here).
tldr.outcome: It gives official Host names as of December 1973, and RFC 603 later updated it.

today: RFC 597 is a dated snapshot with no formal status recorded, and it was updated by RFC 603.

sections.title: What the Maps Show
sections.content:
N. Neigus and J. Feinler attach the latest network maps, geographic and logical, and a list of Hosts. The geographic map shows all IMPs and TIPs installed in the subnetwork. The logical map shows the status of all computers as of 10 December 1973, except MIT-MULTICS, which is shown as moving to IMP #44 from IMP #5.

On the logical map, Hosts with interfaces to the subnet are intersected ovals, a small v is a Very Distant Host (VDH) interface, IMPs are solid black circles and TIPs are circles with a T. Two jagged lines represent satellite links. The names on the map are unofficial IMP names, not official Host names.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two maps, one showing where things are and one showing how they connect.

sections.title: The Host List
sections.content:
The list includes current sites and those projected within the next two months, with an incomplete list of later installations at the end. Each Host's network address is given in octal and decimal. Interfaces from the subnet to the computer appear in parentheses and may be ignored.

A site is a Server or User by self-proclamation. Limited Server means a restricted group of users; dedicated Server means the type of service is restricted. The status column also notes any special operating system, such as TENEX, ITS or Multics.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line gives a computer's number, its name, what kind of computer it is and whether it helps others.

sections.title: Official Names
sections.content:
The RFC contains official Host names as of December 1973. Naming conventions and an official Hostname list will be maintained at the NIC by Jake Feinler and published in the ARPANEWS, with an online version at the NIC and a printed one issued periodically as part of the Resource Notebook. Other sites are encouraged to copy the list to their own systems.

Example entries include UCLA-NMC (Host 1), SRI-ARC (Host 2) and BBN-TENEX (decimal address 69).
sections.plainLanguage: One person keeps the official list of names, and everyone is welcome to copy it.
